title: The Road to Moscow and Back
subtitle: Napoleon's invasion of Russia: the Niemen, Smolensk, Borodino, the burning of Moscow, the retreat, the Berezina, Vilna — 1812
intro: On 24 June 1812 the largest army Europe had yet seen began crossing the Niemen into the Russian Empire. It was French only at its core. Germans from Hesse, Württemberg and Bavaria, Italians, Poles, Swiss, Croats and Portuguese marched with it. Six months later a few tens of thousands of frostbitten men came back over the same river. In between came the summer marches through Lithuania, the burning of Smolensk, the slaughter at Borodino, five weeks in a Moscow that burned around them, and a retreat that became one of the great disasters in military history.

This chapter lines up the people who wrote it down while it was happening, or tried to. A Hessian captain records the hours his company stood under Russian guns and the coffee he took from his dead cook's pocket. Two soldier-artists, a Württemberger and a Bavarian, date their sketches by place and day, so their portfolios read as visual diaries. A bored commissary who would become Stendhal writes to his sister and his friends about lost breeches and lost manuscripts. Napoleon's surgeon writes to his wife from Moscow. Napoleon himself writes to Paris about wine cellars, then about blowing up the Kremlin.

On the other side stand Kutuzov, who called Borodino a victory and then gave up Moscow, and Rostopchin, Moscow's governor, who promised to defend the city, then emptied it and may have set it alight. A nineteen-year-old Guards lieutenant writes and draws his war. A British general at Russian headquarters fumes that the French are being allowed to escape. Inside the occupied city, a French actress and a Russian deacon's wife are left to survive among the looters; both told their stories only years later.

Far away, in the capital Napoleon never reached, the American minister John Quincy Adams reads the bulletins and the rumours and tries to work out the truth. On 15 September, the day the French entered Moscow, his baby daughter died. The scale of the two events could hardly be more different, but they share a date.

These eyes do not agree. The commander's dispatch, the memoirist's set piece and the captain's pencilled hours describe the same days in different worlds. Where entries cluster, at Borodino, in the week of the fire, at Krasnoi, at the Berezina and on the frozen road to Vilna, the reader can watch the gap open between what headquarters believed and what the ranks endured.
calendar_note: Two calendars run through this chapter. In 1812 Russia still used the Julian (Old Style, O.S.) calendar, which was 12 days behind the Gregorian (New Style, N.S.) calendar used by the French, Germans, Italians, Britain and the United States. So the Russian 26 August is the French 7 September (Borodino); 2 September O.S. is 14 September N.S. (the French entry into Moscow); and the Berezina crossing of 26–29 November N.S. was 14–17 November in Russian documents. Russians still mark Borodino Day on 8 September, a later conversion. Every date_iso here is New Style. Where a Russian source or event is involved, date_display gives both dates. John Quincy Adams, writing from St Petersburg, sometimes wrote both himself, as in '12/24 June'. Watch for unconverted dates in older English books that use Russian sources.

eyes.name: Franz Roeder
eyes.role: Captain in the 1st Battalion of the Hessian Lifeguards (Hesse-Darmstadt), in his late thirties
eyes.where: Marched from Kovno to Vitebsk and Smolensk. Held the line through the November retreat (Krasnoi, Orsha). Later captured.
eyes.authenticity: A diary kept day by day during the campaign. A descendant, Helen Roeder, translated it and set it inside her own linking narrative, published as The Ordeal of Captain Roeder (London, 1960; Routledge reprint). Readers should keep her editorial bridges apart from his dated entries.
eyes.bio: A middle-aged professional officer from a small German allied state, writing in pencil through hunger, typhus-like fever and Cossack raids. His November entries are unusually exact: he records hours of artillery fire, the dead cook whose coffee he drank, and the moment he reported sick. His diary is the view from inside a battalion that was dissolving.

sources.title: The Ordeal of Captain Roeder (Routledge Library Editions)
Extract of the November 1812 entries (Weapons and Warfare)

eyes.name: Christian Wilhelm von Faber du Faur
eyes.role: Lieutenant of artillery, 25th (Württemberg) Division, Ney's III Corps, aged 31–32. He had trained as a painter.
eyes.where: With III Corps from the Niemen through Smolensk and Borodino, then back through the retreat to East Prussia
eyes.authenticity: He sketched almost daily in pencil, ink and watercolour, and the sketches were exhibited in 1816. In 1831–44 he published them as lithographic plates, Blätter aus meinem Portefeuille, with commentary by himself and fellow veteran Friedrich von Kausler. The plates are later reworkings, but each caption keeps the place and day of the original sketch.
eyes.bio: Faber du Faur is the campaign's best visual diarist. His captions fix a place and a day, and his drawings show what writers often left out: bivouacs, foraging, dead horses, burned villages, men selling skins for bread. He later rose to general.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Christian Wilhelm von Faber du Faur
With Napoleon in Russia (Greenhill, 2001): review, napoleon.org
National Library of Belarus virtual gallery: Faber du Faur

eyes.name: Albrecht Adam
eyes.role: Bavarian battle painter, aged 26, attached to Prince Eugène de Beauharnais's topographical bureau in IV Corps
eyes.side: Grande Armée, IV Corps (mostly Italian troops, with Bavarians)
eyes.where: With Eugène's corps: Beshenkovichi, Ostrovno, Smolensk, Borodino, Moscow
eyes.vantage_label: staff painter drawing on the spot
eyes.authenticity: He drew in the field and dated many of his sheets; originals survive in the Hermitage and elsewhere. After Eugène's death he worked them up as the lithograph series Voyage pittoresque et militaire (Munich, 1828–33). His oil paintings, such as Napoleon in burning Moscow (1841), were made decades later and are reconstructions, not records.
eyes.bio: A professional artist taken along to record the campaign. His dated field drawings sit beside Faber du Faur's as a second visual diary from a different corps. He knew the Italian and Bavarian troops of IV Corps rather than the Württembergers.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Albrecht Adam

eyes.name: Henri Beyle (Stendhal)
eyes.role: Auditor of the Conseil d'État serving as a commissary officer for army supplies, aged 29
eyes.side: French Empire, civil administration of the army
eyes.where: Followed headquarters from Vilna to Smolensk and Moscow. Sent back to Smolensk on supply duty, then made the retreat to Vilna and Königsberg.
eyes.authenticity: Dated letters to his sister Pauline, his friend Félix Faure and others survive and are printed in his Correspondance. His 1812 journal notebooks are fragmentary and partly lost: he records losing manuscript notes on the retreat. Later autobiographical writing, which adds anecdotes, should be kept separate from the dated letters.
eyes.bio: A future novelist working as a bureaucrat. He writes with ironic detachment, and he worries about breeches and lost books as much as about the army. He watched Moscow burn from just outside the city. On the retreat he is remembered for shaving every day and for finding a ford over the Berezina instead of the crush at the bridges.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Stendhal
Lituanus 1976: Stendhal's journey through Lithuania, with dated letters

eyes.name: Dominique-Jean Larrey
eyes.role: Surgeon-in-chief of the Grande Armée, aged 46
eyes.where: Field hospitals at Borodino, the occupied city of Moscow, the retreat and the Berezina
eyes.authenticity: The Wellcome Collection holds his letters to his wife Charlotte (MS.5316, 1797–1834). Items 82–83 are described as written from Moscow in 1812, one on the burning of the city and one on Borodino. His surgical memoirs (vol. 4, on Russia; English edition Philadelphia, 1832) were written up afterwards. The famous figure of about 200 amputations at Borodino comes from the memoir tradition and is often repeated without a source.
eyes.bio: The inventor of the flying ambulance worked through Borodino amputating, and argued for early amputation to prevent gangrene. On the retreat he studied frostbite and the deaths of men who drank icy water. At the Berezina, soldiers reportedly passed him over their heads to the far bank.

sources.title: Wellcome Collection MS.5316: Letters from Baron Larrey to his wife
Hektoen International: Blood at Borodino

eyes.name: Philippe-Paul, comte de Ségur
eyes.role: General, aide to the imperial headquarters (assistant quartermaster of the palace), aged 32
eyes.where: In the Kremlin with Napoleon during the fire
eyes.authenticity: Histoire de Napoléon et de la Grande Armée pendant l'année 1812 (1824; English 1825) is a literary reconstruction, written a decade later and challenged at once by Gourgaud, who fought him in a duel over it. It is vivid and influential, and Minard used it, but its scenes and speeches should be read as one memoirist's dramatisation.
eyes.bio: Ségur's set pieces, above all Napoleon's escape from the burning Kremlin, shaped how Europe remembered 1812. He is the only eye here standing next to the emperor, and also the one most open to the charge of improving the story.

sources.title: Ségur on the burning of Moscow (Liberty, Equality, Fraternity, GMU)

eyes.name: Napoleon I
eyes.role: Emperor of the French and commander of the Grande Armée, aged 43
eyes.where: Imperial headquarters: Vilna, Smolensk, Borodino, the Moscow Kremlin, then the retreat. Left the army at Smorgon on 5 December.
eyes.authenticity: His dated letters and orders are printed in the Fondation Napoléon's Correspondance générale (vol. 12, 1812), and several originals have come up at auction. The army bulletins were propaganda written for publication. The 29th Bulletin (3 December) was the first to admit disaster.
eyes.bio: The man whose decisions moved half a million others. His own letters show him first treating Moscow as a prize with wine cellars, then threatening the Kremlin as he left. Set beside the diaries of men starving in his columns, they show how far headquarters was from the ranks.

sources.title: Napoleon letter from Moscow, 18 Sept 1812, to Cambacérès (Connexion)
Napoleon letters from the Russian campaign at auction (eNCA/AFP)
Fondation Napoléon: Correspondance générale, 1812 volume

eyes.name: Mikhail Illarionovich Kutuzov
eyes.role: General of infantry, from 17 August (O.S.) commander-in-chief of the Russian armies, aged 66–67
eyes.where: Russian headquarters: Tsaryovo-Zaymishche, Borodino, Fili, the camp at Tarutino, the pursuit
eyes.authenticity: His official reports to Alexander I are printed in the Russian documentary series on Kutuzov and 1812. This chapter could not check the exact wording or date of each report online. The entries below are limited to events that are well documented, and they are marked approximate.
eyes.bio: An old, heavy, cautious commander who called Borodino a victory and then gave up Moscow to save the army. From Tarutino he waited, and let winter and hunger do much of the work. Some allies, including the British commissioner Wilson, called that caution timidity.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mikhail Kutuzov

eyes.name: Count Fyodor Vasilyevich Rostopchin
eyes.side: Russian Empire, civil authority of Moscow
eyes.where: In Moscow until 14 September, then with the army near Tarutino and at his estate at Voronovo
eyes.authenticity: His 1812 voice survives mainly in the patriotic broadsheets (afishki) he had posted in Moscow that summer, in official correspondence, and in his 1823 Paris pamphlet La vérité sur l'incendie de Moscou. In that pamphlet he denied ordering the fire, though he admitted elsewhere that he had ordered destruction. His accounts of himself are partisan and contradictory.
eyes.bio: A showman of patriotism who promised Muscovites the city would be defended, then emptied it: he opened the prisons, removed the fire pumps and left. Whether he lit the fire is still argued. Tolstoy thought a wooden city full of soldiers would burn anyway. He is the eye who most needs cross-examining.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Fyodor Rostopchin
La vérité sur l'incendie de Moscou et d'autres textes (napoleon.org)

eyes.name: Sir Robert Thomas Wilson
eyes.role: British general and liaison officer (British commissioner) at Russian headquarters, aged 35
eyes.where: With Kutuzov's army from Tarutino through Maloyaroslavets, Vyazma and Krasnoi
eyes.authenticity: His Private Diary of Travels, Personal Services, and Public Events (ed. H. Randolph, London: John Murray, 1861) prints his campaign journal. His Narrative of Events during the Invasion of Russia (1860) is a more argued account written later. A modern selection, General Wilson's Journal 1812–1814, was edited by Antony Brett-James (1964). He was openly hostile to Kutuzov.
eyes.bio: An English eye inside the Russian camp, who pushed constantly for a more aggressive pursuit. He was present at Maloyaroslavets, Vyazma and Krasnoi, and saw Rostopchin burn his own house. His diary gives the Russian side of the retreat as seen by an ally who thought it too slow.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Robert Wilson (British Army officer)
Private Diary (1861), National Library of Belarus catalogue record

eyes.name: John Quincy Adams
eyes.role: United States Minister to Russia, aged 45
eyes.side: United States (neutral in the Franco-Russian war, itself at war with Britain from June 1812)
eyes.where: St Petersburg, about 700 km from Moscow, hearing bulletins and rumour
eyes.authenticity: Letters to his parents and brother, printed and online in the Adams Papers (Founders Online). He also kept a full diary, held by the Massachusetts Historical Society. He dates in the Gregorian style and sometimes writes both dates, for example 12/24 June.
eyes.bio: An American watching the war from the enemy capital Napoleon never reached. His letters weigh Russian bulletins against rumour. On 15 September, the day the French entered Moscow, his infant daughter died, and his letters join private grief to public catastrophe.

sources.title: JQA to Thomas Boylston Adams, 4 July 1812
JQA to Thomas Boylston Adams, 29 September 1812
JQA to John Adams, 4 October 1812
JQA to Abigail Adams, 30 November 1812

eyes.name: Louise Fusil
eyes.role: French actress in the French theatre company resident in Moscow, about 40
eyes.where: Inside Moscow during the occupation and fire. She left with the retreating army in October.
eyes.authenticity: Her Souvenirs d'une actrice (Paris, 1841) include the Moscow and retreat chapters. Her account of the retreat circulated earlier, from 1817. Scholars note serious factual and chronological errors, so treat it as a recollection, not a dated record.
eyes.bio: A woman and a civilian, French but long settled in Russia. She performed for the occupiers, met Rostopchin and Caulaincourt, and then fled with the army. She rescued a child abandoned at Krasnoi and crossed the Berezina in Marshal Berthier's carriage. Her view is of non-combatants caught between two armies.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Louise Fusil

eyes.name: Elena Alekseevna Pokhorskaya
eyes.role: Wife of the deacon Dmitri Vlasievich Pokhorsky of a Moscow parish church
eyes.vantage_label: Muscovite who stayed, a victim of the occupation
eyes.authenticity: This is not a diary. It is an oral recollection she gave decades later, gathered with other Muscovites' accounts in Rasskazy ochevidtsev o dvenadtsatom gode (Moscow, 1872–73), compiled from the Moskovskie vedomosti, and summarised in French in the Revue des Deux Mondes. It is flagged as late and remembered.
eyes.bio: One of the few ordinary Russian women of the occupied city whose voice was written down at all. Her family believed Rostopchin's promises until the French arrived. Her account has none of the strategy that fills the officers' writing: it is about a household, a torn proclamation and a child.

sources.title: La grande Armée à Moscou d'après les récits de témoins moscovites (Wikisource)

eyes.name: Alexander Vasilyevich Chicherin
eyes.role: Lieutenant in the Semenovsky Life Guards regiment, aged 19
eyes.where: With the Guards through Borodino, the retreat past Moscow and the pursuit west
eyes.authenticity: A journal of 1812–13 illustrated with the author's own drawings, published in 1966 without the illustrations (Dnevnik Aleksandra Chicherina, 1812–1813). Recent scholarship reads it as a deliberately literary text that borrows from Sterne and Chateaubriand. This chapter could not check individual entry dates online, so it includes only one approximate entry.
eyes.bio: A cultivated young aristocrat who wrote and drew his war at the same time. He is the Russian counterpart to Faber du Faur and Adam. He died of wounds received at Kulm in 1813, so the diary is his entire adult record.

sources.title: The Illustrated Manuscript by A. V. Chicherin (Universe of Humanities, 2015)

entries.headline: News reaches the embassy: the French have crossed the Niemen
entries.digest: Writing ten days later, Adams records the invasion with both calendars side by side: on 12/24 June the French crossed the Niemen at four points. His latest bulletins, of 17/29 June, report no major action yet, and he expects a decisive battle between two huge armies. For now the capital simply waits.
entries.source_note: JQA to Thomas Boylston Adams, 4 July 1812 (Founders Online)

entries.place: Kirgaliczky, near Suderva (Lithuania), on the road beyond Vilna
entries.headline: First week in Russia: III Corps camps in Lithuanian woods
entries.digest: One of Faber du Faur's early plates is captioned with this place and day, six days after the crossing. III Corps was moving through Lithuania toward Vilna in heat and rain, and the supply train was already falling behind. His first sheets show a summer march, not yet a catastrophe.
entries.source_note: Plate caption 'Kirgaliczky, Suderva, 30 June 1812' (heritage print listing). Faber du Faur, Blätter aus meinem Portefeuille im Laufe des Feldzugs 1812 (1831–44); English edition With Napoleon in Russia, ed. J. North (2001). The date is in the plate caption.

entries.headline: The Hessians reach Vitebsk and settle in
entries.digest: Roeder's battalion marched from Kovno to Vitebsk and spent a stretch of the summer there. His diary of these weeks is about billets, sickness among the men and the hunt for food in a country the Russians had stripped. At this point the campaign still looked like an ordinary war.
entries.source_note: Helen Roeder, The Ordeal of Captain Roeder (1960), chapters 'The March to Vitebsk' and 'Vitebsk' (table of contents, Routledge listing).

entries.place: Beshenkovichi (Biešankovičy), on the Dvina, at the Khreptovich manor
entries.headline: Adam draws the manor where Eugène's headquarters halted
entries.digest: Adam dated this field drawing of Beshenkovichi on the Dvina, where Eugène's IV Corps came up with Napoleon's main body before the fighting at Ostrovno. It is a quiet sheet: a manor, a river town, troops at rest. It records the army still in good order, a month into Russia.
entries.source_note: Wikimedia Commons file titled 'Biešankovičy, Chraptovič (A. Adam, 24.07.1812)' (seen in search results; the file page itself did not load).

entries.headline: First battle of Krasnoi: Ney and Murat strike Neverovsky
entries.digest: Faber du Faur's plate is captioned for the first battle at Krasnoi, where Ney's corps and Murat's cavalry caught Neverovsky's division. The Russians withdrew in squares along the Smolensk road. Three months later the same town would be a trap for the retreating French.
entries.source_note: Plate caption 'Battle of Krasnoi, August 14, 1812'. Faber du Faur, Blätter aus meinem Portefeuille im Laufe des Feldzugs 1812 (1831–44); English edition With Napoleon in Russia, ed. J. North (2001). The date is in the plate caption.

entries.headline: Adam records Smolensk burning after the assault
entries.digest: Adam's image of the battle of Smolensk is dated 18 August, the day after the main assault, as the Russians left the burning city. Smolensk was the first great Russian town the army took, and the first to be given up in flames. The fire foreshadowed Moscow.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Albrecht Adam (image caption 'Battle of Smolensk, 18 August 1812'). The plate may be a later lithograph after a field sketch.

entries.headline: Stendhal writes to Félix Faure from captured Smolensk
entries.digest: Having caught up with imperial headquarters, Beyle writes to his friend Félix Faure from Smolensk. He describes the hardships since Vilna, including the loss of his calash, his light carriage. The tone is weary irony: the commissary sees the army's poverty more clearly than its glory.
entries.source_note: Letter to Félix Faure, Smolensk, 24 Aug 1812, summarised in Lituanus 1976 (no. 2).

entries.place: In woods about 60 leagues from Moscow
entries.headline: In a forest, Beyle traces the army's misery back to Vilna
entries.digest: Writing in the woods on the road east, Beyle thinks back over the march. He dates his sense of the army's misery to Vilna, where the disorder and hunger first became visible. Ten days before Borodino, the future novelist is already writing about decline.
entries.source_note: Stendhal, letter/notes of 28 Aug 1812, summarised in Lituanus 1976.

entries.place: Near Gzhatsk, on the Moscow road
entries.headline: Approaching the Kolocha: the eve of the great battle
entries.digest: Faber du Faur's caption fixes this sheet at Gzhatsk on 5 September, the day the French took the Shevardino redoubt ahead of the Russian line. Troops fed and foraged in a stripped landscape while both armies drew up near Borodino. Two days before the battle, his plates are about weather, mud and waiting.
entries.source_note: Plate caption 'Gzhatsk, September 5, 1812' (heritage print listing). Faber du Faur, Blätter aus meinem Portefeuille im Laufe des Feldzugs 1812 (1831–44); English edition With Napoleon in Russia, ed. J. North (2001). The date is in the plate caption.

entries.place: Borodino, with III Corps before the Bagration flèches and Semenovskoye
entries.headline: Borodino: Faber draws the guns at the flèches
entries.digest: Faber du Faur's Borodino plate shows the Württemberg artillery in action on the ground where Ney's corps fought for the Bagration flèches. Here the battle is smoke, wheels, gun crews and dead horses, not maps or marshals. Bridgeman lists it as a colour lithograph from his published series.
entries.source_note: Faber du Faur, 'The Battle of Borodino', colour lithograph (Bridgeman Images listing). Faber du Faur, Blätter aus meinem Portefeuille im Laufe des Feldzugs 1812 (1831–44); English edition With Napoleon in Russia, ed. J. North (2001). The date is in the plate caption.

entries.place: Dressing stations behind the French centre, Borodino
entries.headline: Larrey amputates through the bloodiest day of the wars
entries.digest: Larrey ran the main dressing stations through the day and night, pressing his doctrine of fast amputation before gangrene set in. Later tradition credits him with some two hundred operations in about a day, a figure that sources repeat but rarely cite. His own letter to his wife about the battle, written from Moscow, is in the Wellcome archive.
entries.source_note: Hektoen International and hekint.org on Larrey ('reportedly 200 operations in one day'). Wellcome MS.5316 item 83 (letter from Moscow describing Borodino).

entries.place: With the Semenovsky Guards in the Russian reserve, Borodino
entries.headline: A nineteen-year-old Guards lieutenant under the bombardment
entries.digest: The Semenovsky regiment stood in the Guards reserve and was drawn into the fighting near Semenovskoye, under heavy artillery fire. Chicherin's illustrated diary covers the battle from inside a regiment that held its ground. This chapter could not check the exact wording of his entry, so only his presence and the regiment's role are given here.
entries.source_note: Dnevnik Aleksandra Chicherina 1812–1813 (Moscow, 1966). On the manuscript: Universe of Humanities 2015 article (NSU).

entries.place: Russian headquarters, Borodino, then on the Mozhaisk road
entries.headline: Kutuzov reports Borodino to the tsar as a victory
entries.digest: Having held most of his line and kept the army in being, Kutuzov reported to Alexander I that he had won. His losses were in fact heavier than Napoleon's, and on 8 September he withdrew toward Moscow. Alexander celebrated, and on 30 August (O.S.), 11 September (N.S.), promoted him to field marshal.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Mikhail Kutuzov (report of victory; promotion 11 Sept N.S. / 30 Aug O.S.). Exact dispatch date not checked.

entries.headline: The governor empties his city and rides out
entries.digest: After the council at Fili decided to give up Moscow without a fight, Rostopchin did the opposite of what his broadsheets had promised. He had most remaining residents evacuated, opened the prisons and asylums, and, by many accounts, removed the fire pumps and left police with incendiary orders. He left the city himself on the day the French entered.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Fyodor Rostopchin (left Moscow 14 Sept 1812). Wikipedia: Fire of Moscow (1812).

entries.headline: The deacon tears up Rostopchin's proclamation
entries.digest: Her husband the deacon had trusted the governor's posted promises that Moscow would be defended. When French soldiers appeared in the streets, he tore the proclamation up in shock and anger. Her memory of the day is a domestic one: a household that stayed because officials told it to, and found itself in occupied streets.
entries.source_note: Testimony of H. A. Pokhorskaya in Tolycheva, Rasskazy ochevidtsev (1872–73), via Revue des Deux Mondes article (Wikisource). The exact day is inferred from the French entry.

entries.headline: Officers wake to see palaces burning beyond the Kremlin
entries.digest: Napoleon entered the Kremlin feeling his ambition satisfied, while the fire seemed limited to the bazaar. Around midnight two officers woke to see palaces ablaze, and a north wind drove the flames toward the Kremlin where the Guard slept. Ségur records French suspicion of deliberate Russian arson, with men and women seen with torches. He also admits that drunken, looting soldiers may have started fires.
entries.source_note: Ségur, History of the Expedition to Russia (London, 1825), II, 38–48, via revolution.chnm.org/d/522. Memoir written c. 1824.

entries.headline: In St Petersburg, Adams's infant daughter dies
entries.digest: Far from the front, the Adams household lost its baby daughter Louisa. Adams later called it the hardest blow of his life. Writing to his father, he noted that the French entered Moscow on the same day, 15 September: two catastrophes of very different size, joined by a date.
entries.source_note: JQA to John Adams, 4 October 1812 (Founders Online).

entries.headline: An actress watches looters work through the burning streets
entries.digest: Fusil stayed in Moscow and saw the city burn around its remaining foreign residents. She later wrote of French soldiers looting houses, and she places the start of the fire in Petrovka Street. She had to find shelter and protection from Caulaincourt's people, in a city that belonged to no one.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Louise Fusil; Wikipedia: Fire of Moscow (1812) (Fusil places origin in Petrovka). Memoir Souvenirs d'une actrice (1841).

entries.place: Kremlin, escaping through a postern toward the Petrovsky Palace
entries.headline: Napoleon's headquarters escapes the Kremlin through the fire
entries.digest: As the flames ringed the Kremlin, Napoleon finally agreed to leave. Ségur describes the staff going out through a narrow postern and down streets so thick with fire that the escape was nearly cut off, before they reached the Petrovsky Palace outside the city. In his telling the emperor felt outmatched by a people willing to burn their own capital.
entries.source_note: Ségur (1825), II, 38–48 (revolution.chnm.org/d/522). The day of the move to Petrovsky is the standard date.

entries.headline: The commissary watches Moscow burn from outside the city
entries.digest: Beyle watched the fire from just outside the city and wrote about it in letters home. He took a lofty, almost aesthetic view of the disaster, while also noting the looting and the quick shifts of fortune among the officials. His letters treat the fire as both a spectacle and a supply problem.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Stendhal (watched the burning of Moscow from just outside the city). Exact letter dates not checked online.

entries.headline: Napoleon to Cambacérès: the fire dies down, cellars intact
entries.digest: Back in the Kremlin as the fire burned out, Napoleon wrote to his arch-chancellor Cambacérès in Paris. He had toured the main quarters and found more than half the city burned. He also found well-stocked wine and spirit cellars he expected the army to use. The letter is calm and practical: he is taking stock of a prize he has not yet realised is a trap.
entries.source_note: Letter of 18 Sept 1812 to Cambacérès, sold at auction (Connexion France; eNCA/AFP).

entries.headline: Larrey writes home about Moscow in flames
entries.digest: From the occupied city, Larrey wrote to his wife about the burning of Moscow, and separately about Borodino. He described the fire as many small fires that joined into a single blaze driven from the northeast. He was also running hospitals in a city full of wounded from the battle.
entries.source_note: Wellcome Collection MS.5316 items 82–83 ('From Moscow, 1812'). Wikipedia: Fire of Moscow (Larrey's description).

entries.headline: A child lost in the occupied, starving city
entries.digest: Pokhorskaya recalled that her infant died during the occupation, in a burned city where food, fuel and safety were all scarce. Other parish witnesses gathered in the same collection describe icons stripped of silver and a killing at a well. Her loss stands for the many Muscovite deaths that no bulletin counted.
entries.source_note: Tolycheva, Rasskazy ochevidtsev (1872–73), via Revue des Deux Mondes (Wikisource).

entries.headline: Moscow lost, yet Petersburg is not discouraged
entries.digest: Cut off from American mail by two wars, Adams writes that the French have held Moscow for weeks after several bloody but indecisive battles. He finds the Russian people and government not dismayed: they think the French position is desperate. He says little more, guessing that his letters may be opened.
entries.source_note: JQA to Thomas Boylston Adams, 29 September 1812 (Founders Online).

entries.headline: Kutuzov digs in at Tarutino and waits
entries.digest: Kutuzov's army reached its camp at Tarutino, astride the roads to the grain-rich south. He rested and reinforced the army, refused major battle and let Napoleon wait in the ruins for a peace that never came. Critics at headquarters, Wilson among them, wanted him to attack.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Mikhail Kutuzov (arrived Tarutino 3 Oct). Underlying dispatches not checked.

entries.headline: Adams weighs Borodino's victory claims against Moscow's fall
entries.digest: Writing to his father, Adams sets the official story against the facts. Petersburg celebrated Borodino as a victory and made Kutuzov field marshal, yet days later Napoleon walked into Moscow. Adams thinks Russian generals too cautious, but he sees Napoleon deep in hostile country with half his army gone. He notes that rumour and bulletins distort events, so America may know the truth better than Russia does.
entries.source_note: JQA to John Adams, 4 October 1812 (Founders Online).

entries.place: Voronovo, his country estate near Tarutino
entries.headline: Rostopchin burns his own mansion rather than shelter the French
entries.digest: Rostopchin set fire to his own estate at Voronovo rather than leave it to the enemy, reportedly in front of the British commissioner Robert Wilson. Some accounts say he left a notice for the French explaining the act. It was the scorched-earth gesture he would later partly deny for Moscow itself.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Fire of Moscow (1812): 'set fire to his own estate near Tarutino on 5 October, in the presence of Robert Wilson'. Calendar of the source date unclear.

entries.headline: The British commissioner watches the governor fire his house
entries.digest: Wilson's journal records riding with Rostopchin and seeing him burn Voronovo. For an English officer it was a striking sign of Russian resolve, the opposite of the negotiated peace Napoleon hoped for. Wilson used such scenes to argue that Russia would fight on.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Fire of Moscow (1812). Wilson, Private Diary (1861). Exact entry date not checked.

entries.headline: Beyle asks Kovno for cloth to make new breeches
entries.digest: Four days before the army left, Beyle wrote from Moscow to Noue, the commissary at Kovno, asking for cloth for breeches. Noue had died on 13 October, two days before. The letter, sent to a dead man about trousers, captures how badly headquarters understood its own position.
entries.source_note: Stendhal to Noue, Moscow, 15 Oct 1812, summarised in Lituanus 1976.

entries.headline: Napoleon orders Kremlin towers and walls blown up
entries.digest: As the army left Moscow, Napoleon wrote that he would destroy several towers and sections of the Kremlin walls. Mortier's rear guard set the mines, and parts of the Kremlin were badly damaged. Five weeks after admiring the city, he is ordering demolitions.
entries.source_note: Napoleon letter of 20 Oct 1812 (eNCA/AFP auction report).

entries.headline: At Maloyaroslavets the road south is closed
entries.digest: Wilson was present as Eugène's IV Corps and Dokhturov's Russians fought over the burning town of Maloyaroslavets, which changed hands repeatedly. The French held the ruins, but Kutuzov stood across the road to the south. Napoleon turned back to the devastated Smolensk road, the decision that doomed the army.
entries.source_note: napoleon.org biography of Wilson (present at Maloyaroslavets, Viazma, Krasnyi). Wilson, Private Diary (1861). Entry wording not checked.

entries.headline: Vyazma: the retreat begins to break apart
entries.digest: At Vyazma the Russians struck the French rear guard and Wilson saw the columns giving way. He saw Russian chances to destroy whole corps, and was angry when they were let pass. The first frosts were beginning.
entries.source_note: napoleon.org biography of Wilson (present at Viazma). Wilson, Private Diary (1861).

entries.headline: Sent ahead to Smolensk to prepare stores, Beyle turns west
entries.digest: Beyle had been sent to Smolensk to gather food for the returning army, and from there he turned back toward Paris. Smolensk's magazines became a scene of riot as starving units arrived and plundered them. The commissary's job had become impossible.
entries.source_note: Lituanus 1976 (turned back toward Paris from Smolensk, 11 Nov). Wikipedia: Stendhal (sent to Smolensk to prepare provisions).

entries.headline: Three hours under Russian guns, and the cook falls
entries.digest: The Hessians marched at 3 a.m. with Roeder's company down to seven sergeants and 27 men. From about half past nine to half past twelve they stood under Russian artillery. His old cook Heck was killed, and Roeder ate sugar and barley coffee taken from Heck's pocket and from a dead French officer. Around one o'clock they were withdrawn.
entries.source_note: Roeder diary, 17 Nov 1812 (Weapons and Warfare extract of The Ordeal of Captain Roeder).

entries.headline: Krasnoi: Kutuzov lets the Guard march past
entries.digest: Wilson was with the Russians at Krasnoi, where for several days they mauled corps after corps of the retreating army and nearly cut off Ney. He thought a full attack could have captured Napoleon himself, and blamed Kutuzov's caution for missing it. On the other side of the same field, Roeder was counting his men.
entries.source_note: napoleon.org biography of Wilson (present at Krasnyi). Wilson, Private Diary (1861).

entries.headline: An actress picks up a child abandoned in the snow
entries.digest: Travelling with General Lefebvre's party, Fusil saw the fighting at Krasnoi. She later told how she twice picked up a small child its mother had left behind. Her memoir records the deaths of people and horses and the Cossack raids, as a civilian among the soldiers.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Louise Fusil (Krasnoi, the abandoned child). Memoir (1841) with known chronological errors.

entries.headline: Sick at the Orsha bridge, Roeder hears his groom is dead
entries.digest: Very ill, Roeder crossed the Dnieper at Orsha and met Colonel Follenius, who told the officers the army would split onto three roads. An attempt to seize flour and brandy failed because the men got drunk. His servant Dietrich turned up with his belongings, and Roeder learned that his groom had died after Smolensk. His horse slipped on the bridge but was saved.
entries.source_note: Roeder diary, 20 Nov 1812 (Weapons and Warfare extract).

entries.headline: Cossacks take a wagon in plain view; Roeder reports sick
entries.digest: Cossacks seized a wagon and two horses in full view of the brigade. After about seven hours' march and a river crossing, the unit bivouacked at Kokhanovo, and Roeder, close to collapse, reported sick. It is a short, flat entry from a man running out of strength.
entries.source_note: Roeder diary, 21 Nov 1812 (Weapons and Warfare extract).

entries.headline: Passed over the soldiers' heads at the Berezina bridge
entries.digest: Larrey crossed the Berezina more than once to bring medical stores over. When panic broke out on the bridge, soldiers who recognised him lifted him and passed him over their heads to the far bank, an episode told in the biographical tradition. He also studied the cold, noting deaths among men who drank snow or icy water.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Dominique Jean Larrey; hekint.org. Based on memoir and later biography, not a dated letter.

entries.headline: Beyle avoids the bridges and finds a ford
entries.digest: Instead of joining the crush at Eblé's two pontoon bridges, Beyle and his companions found a usable ford. That choice probably saved their lives. He also kept his carriage and his habits, reportedly shaving every day of the retreat.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Stendhal (ford over the Berezina; shaving daily).

entries.headline: Across the Berezina in Marshal Berthier's carriage
entries.digest: Fusil crossed the river in the carriage of Marshal Berthier, Napoleon's chief of staff, a privilege that set her apart from the thousands of civilians left behind. When Eblé burned the bridges on the morning of 29 November, a mass of stragglers and camp followers was still on the east bank. Her escape and their fate came out of the same hours.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: Louise Fusil (Berthier's carriage). Wikipedia: Battle of Berezina (bridges burned 29 Nov, 8:30 a.m.).

entries.headline: From Petersburg: a starving, almost naked army
entries.digest: Adams gives his mother the outline: invasion on 24 June, Moscow on 15 September, six weeks in the ruins, retreat from 28 October. He reports famine, frost, more than 30,000 prisoners in ten days and the loss of the artillery. He predicts the rest will surrender within days and wonders whether Napoleon is alive. He also expects risings in Germany, Italy and France, with Russia becoming the arbiter of Europe. He does not yet know about the Berezina.
entries.source_note: JQA to Abigail Adams, 30 November 1812 (Founders Online).

entries.headline: The 29th Bulletin admits the army has been destroyed
entries.digest: From Molodechno, Napoleon issued the 29th Bulletin, the first public admission of disaster. It blamed the cold for the loss of the cavalry, artillery and transport. It closed by assuring France that the emperor's health had never been better.
entries.quote: His Majesty's health has never been better.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia: French invasion of Russia (29th Bulletin, 3 Dec 1812).

entries.headline: Near Smorgon: the march in deep frost
entries.digest: Faber du Faur's plate dated 3 December places him near Smorgon in the worst of the cold, on the same day the 29th Bulletin was issued a few miles away. The remnants of III Corps had stopped being a formation. His captions here mark only place and day; the drawings show what that meant.
entries.source_note: Plate caption 'Near Smarhon, December 3, 1812' (heritage print listing). Faber du Faur, Blätter aus meinem Portefeuille im Laufe des Feldzugs 1812 (1831–44); English edition With Napoleon in Russia, ed. J. North (2001). The date is in the plate caption.

entries.headline: At Molodechno, Beyle loses his manuscript on Italian painting
entries.digest: On the road to Vilna, Beyle lost the manuscript notes for his history of Italian painting, a book he had been carrying through the campaign. Among the dead and dying, the writer records a loss of his own. He would rewrite the book later.
entries.source_note: Lituanus 1976 (lost at Maladechno, 4 Dec).

entries.headline: Safe in Vilna for a night, Beyle writes to his sister
entries.digest: Beyle reached Vilna on the evening of the 6th and wrote to his sister Pauline on the 7th before moving on toward Gumbinnen. The city where he had first seen the army's misery in June was now filling with frozen survivors. Its hospitals soon became places of horror he described years later.
entries.source_note: Lituanus 1976 (Vilna, 6–7 Dec; letter to his sister dated 7 Dec).

entries.place: Between Braunsberg and Elbing, East Prussia
entries.headline: Out of Russia: the last plate, on the Prussian road
entries.digest: The final plate of Faber du Faur's series is captioned as a scene between Braunsberg and Elbing on 21 December. The survivors are on German roads among people who would soon change sides. His portfolio of the campaign begins in a Lithuanian summer and ends in a Prussian winter.
entries.source_note: Napoleonguide review of With Napoleon in Russia (last plate 'between Braunsberg and Elbing, 21 December').

entries.headline: From Königsberg, Beyle counts the cost of the march
entries.digest: Resting in Königsberg, Beyle wrote describing the losses since Vilna and the fifty-day march from Moscow, from which he had saved little but his clothes. Two days later he left by sledge for Danzig. In a later autobiography he tells of the ice giving way under his sledge near Königsberg as he fled Cossacks.
entries.source_note: Lituanus 1976 (Königsberg letter of 28 Dec; departure 30 Dec).

entries.headline: Rostopchin denies he burned Moscow
entries.digest: Living in Paris, Rostopchin published La vérité sur l'incendie de Moscou, denying that he had ordered the fire. Elsewhere he admitted ordering destruction. French veterans and Russian officers answered him in print, and the argument over who burned Moscow continued for decades.
entries.source_note: napoleon.org on La vérité sur l'incendie de Moscou (1823); Wikipedia: Fyodor Rostopchin.

convergences.label: The crossing of the Niemen
convergences.note: Adams hears of the crossing through the bulletins and writes both calendars; within a week Faber du Faur is sketching III Corps' bivouacs in Lithuania. The news from far away and the record on the ground start at the same moment.

convergences.label: Borodino (26 August O.S.)
convergences.note: A Württemberg gunner draws the flèches, the French surgeon amputates behind the centre, a Russian Guards lieutenant stands under the same guns from the other side, and the Russian commander reports a victory. Four eyes, no agreement on what the day meant.

convergences.label: Entry into Moscow and the outbreak of the fire (14–18 Sept)
convergences.note: The governor rides out, a deacon tears up his proclamation, Ségur watches palaces burn from the Kremlin, an actress dodges looters, Stendhal watches from outside the city, Napoleon writes about cellars, Larrey writes to his wife. In St Petersburg, Adams's daughter dies the same day. The heart of the chapter: the same fire as betrayal, spectacle, logistics and grief.

convergences.label: Voronovo burns
convergences.note: The man accused of burning Moscow sets fire to his own house in front of a British witness. One sees patriotic sacrifice, the other evidence that Russia will not make peace.

convergences.label: Krasnoi (15–18 November)
convergences.note: From the French side, Roeder counts hours under artillery and his dead cook; from the Russian side, Wilson rages that Kutuzov is letting the Guard escape; between them, Fusil picks a child out of the snow. The same field from three distances.

convergences.label: The Berezina (26–29 November)
convergences.note: The surgeon is passed over men's heads, the commissary finds a ford, the actress rides in a marshal's carriage, while those without rank burn with the bridges. In Petersburg, Adams predicts surrender within days but does not yet know of the crossing.

convergences.label: The 29th Bulletin and the road to Vilna
convergences.note: Napoleon admits disaster and announces his health is excellent. On the same road and the same day, Faber du Faur dates a sketch near Smorgon, and the next day Stendhal loses his manuscript at Molodechno.

ties.note: Wilson was present when Rostopchin burned his Voronovo estate in early October 1812.
Fusil's memoir records her contacts with Rostopchin, governor of the city she stayed in.
Allies on paper and opponents at headquarters: Wilson constantly attacked Kutuzov's cautious pursuit, in his diary and to the tsar.
At Krasnoi in mid-November, Roeder was under the guns Wilson was urging the Russians to push harder.
The two German soldier-artists of 1812, from Württemberg and Bavaria, each turned dated field sketches into lithographic series in the 1820s–40s and created the campaign's visual record.
Ségur served at imperial headquarters and claims to describe Napoleon's escape from the burning Kremlin first-hand.
The two commanders never met. Kutuzov refused Napoleon's peace overtures from Tarutino.
Both were French officials in occupied Moscow and on the same retreat. One wrote as an ironic administrator, the other as a surgeon.
Adams discusses the field-marshal's baton given to Kutuzov after Borodino and judges Russian generalship too cautious.
Two officer-diarists who drew as well as wrote, at Borodino on opposite sides of the Semenovskoye ground.

threads_out.note: The Grande Armée was the Revolution's mass conscript army grown to continental scale, and Napoleon, Larrey and Ségur were all products of the revolutionary decade. Larrey's flying ambulances date from the Army of the Rhine in 1792.
The Old Style calendar that splits every date in this chapter stayed in Russian use until the Bolsheviks abolished it in February 1918. That is why the 'October' Revolution falls in November.

In 1941 Hitler launched Barbarossa two days short of the anniversary of Napoleon's crossing, and Soviet propaganda deliberately called the struggle the Great Patriotic War, after the Patriotic War of 1812. The Borodino field was fought over again in October 1941.
John Quincy Adams, the US minister in this chapter, later led the fight in Congress against the gag rule on anti-slavery petitions, one of the long fuses of the sectional crisis.

The burning of Moscow, Tolstoy's War and Peace (drawing on Moscow witness accounts and memoirs like these) and Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture turned this campaign into a lasting myth of national survival. Minard's chart of the shrinking army is among the most reproduced information graphics ever made.

images.title: The Battle of Borodino
images.caption: Faber du Faur's plate of the battle of 7 September 1812, worked up from his field sketch with Ney's III Corps. It shows the gunners' view rather than the marshals'.
images.credit: Christian Wilhelm von Faber du Faur / Bridgeman Images

images.title: Faber du Faur plates of 1812 in Belarus
images.caption: The National Library of Belarus gallery of Faber du Faur's dated plates from the road through present-day Belarus, from Vitebsk and Orsha to Borisov and Smorgon, much of it the same ground as Roeder's November entries.

images.title: Napoleon in burning Moscow
images.caption: Albrecht Adam painted this scene in 1841, nearly thirty years after the drawings he made in the city. It is a reconstruction, to set beside Ségur's equally retrospective prose.

images.title: Fire of Moscow, 1812
images.caption: A later Russian painting of the fire that consumed most of the wooden city from 14 to 18 September 1812. Who started it is still argued.

images.title: Napoleon's Retreat from Moscow
images.caption: Adolph Northen's 1851 painting fixed the popular image of the retreat: the emperor on the snowy road, his army fading behind him.

images.title: Figurative map of the successive losses in men of the French Army in the Russian campaign 1812–1813
images.caption: Charles Joseph Minard's 1869 chart: the tan band of men entering Russia narrows to the thin black band that returns, plotted against the retreat's temperatures. Minard built it from Thiers, Ségur, Fezensac, Chambray and the unpublished diary of the army pharmacist Jacob.

vantage_key: 0 = principal actor or direct victim (emperor, commander, governor, a Muscovite left in the city); 1 = on campaign or inside Moscow as an eyewitness; 2 = near the front; 3 = elsewhere in Russia or France; 4 = abroad or reading bulletins (Adams in St Petersburg is placed here as a foreign diplomat on news only).
